$comment: Eight Washington local minimum wages, all above the country's highest state rate ($17.13). Two of them -- Renton and Everett -- step MID-YEAR on July 1 for their mid-size employer tier, which is the single most common way a Washington payroll run goes wrong. No Washington jurisdiction, state or local, permits a tip credit.

jurisdictions.name: Seattle
jurisdictions.coverage: All employers regardless of size. Seattle's employer-size tiers, and the old ability of small employers to count tips or medical-benefit payments toward minimum compensation, both ENDED on 2025-01-01.

sources.title: City of Seattle Office of Labor Standards -- Minimum Wage Ordinance
sources.verifiedBy: Fetched and read directly this session: '$21.30' effective January 1, 2026, and 'Starting January 1, 2025, all employers, regardless of schedule size, will be required to pay the same minimum wage.'

jurisdictions.name: SeaTac
jurisdictions.coverage: HOSPITALITY AND TRANSPORTATION employers only -- SeaTac's ordinance is sector-limited, unlike every other Washington local rate. Other SeaTac employers owe the state rate ($17.13).

jurisdictions.name: Tukwila
jurisdictions.coverage: Employers with 15 or more employees worldwide and a Tukwila presence, employers with $2 million or more in Tukwila revenue, or qualifying franchisees.

jurisdictions.name: Burien

variants.label: Employers with 20 or fewer employees
variants.test: NOT COVERED by the Burien ordinance -- the Washington state rate ($17.13) applies.

jurisdictions.note: Burien's ordinance has been the subject of competing measures and litigation since a February 2025 voter initiative; the figures here are the ones Washington L&I publishes as currently in effect.

variants.label: Employers with 15-500 employees, July 1 - December 31, 2026
variants.test: A MID-YEAR step: Renton's mid-size tier catches up to the large-employer rate on 2026-07-01. As of this file's asOf date (2026-09-08) the $21.57 figure is the live one for mid-size employers.

variants.label: Employers with 14 or fewer employees
variants.test: NOT COVERED -- the state rate applies.

variants.label: Employers with 15-499 employees (or over $2M Everett revenue), January 1 - June 30, 2026
Employers with 15-499 employees (or over $2M Everett revenue), July 1 - December 31, 2026
variants.test: A MID-YEAR step, like Renton's. Live as of this file's asOf date.

variants.label: Employers with 14 or fewer employees
variants.test: NOT COVERED -- the state rate applies.

jurisdictions.name: Bellingham
jurisdictions.note: Bellingham's ordinance is defined as the Washington state minimum wage PLUS $2.00, so it moves automatically with the state rate ($17.13 + $2.00 = $19.13).

jurisdictions.name: King County (unincorporated areas only)
jurisdictions.coverage: Employers with 500 or more employees, for work performed in UNINCORPORATED King County only. Seattle, Tukwila, Burien, Renton and SeaTac are incorporated cities with their own ordinances above.

variants.label: Employers with 15 or fewer employees and $2 million or more in annual gross revenue
Employers with 15 or fewer employees and under $2 million in annual gross revenue

jurisdictions.note: The three reduced tiers are a temporary phase-in that ends in 2031, when every employer pays the single county rate.

sources.title: Washington State Department of Labor & Industries -- Local Minimum Wage Rates
sources.verifiedBy: Fetched and read directly this session. L&I's own consolidated table is the primary source for every Washington local rate and tier in this file -- and it CORRECTED two figures that a secondary search had returned wrong (Burien $21.63, not $21.78; Renton's Level 2 mid-year step).

sources.title: UC Berkeley Labor Center -- Inventory of US City and County Minimum Wage Ordinances
sources.verifiedBy: Fetched and read directly this session. The standing national census of local minimum wage ordinances -- used here to establish WHICH jurisdictions exist (so none is silently omitted), with each rate then cross-checked against a second source.

knownGaps: Tacoma repealed its local ordinance in December 2019 once the state rate overtook it; it is deliberately absent rather than carried at $0.
Burien's ordinance remains subject to litigation arising from competing 2025 ballot measures. L&I's published figures are used; a court ruling could change them mid-year.
SeaTac's ordinance covers only hospitality and transportation employers; the precise industry test is in the ordinance and is not modelled here.
